articles.title: Musk Joins 'Axis of Evil' Over Starlink Control
articles.content: Every day, the Ukraine Battlefield update newsletter offers a clear look at how the war is unfolding on the ground. Subscribe for free here to get the full text delivered to your inbox. Trump’s America is becoming a rogue state. The Russians are making a mockery of Trump’s energy ceasefire. What the restrictions on Starlink mean and how they are being felt. The Russians are pushing towards Dobropillia. The 3rd Army Corps reported on the next phase of Operation Vivaldi, but we learned nothing new. Maps of the day — Lyman, Dobropillia Videos of the day — a drone hit a flying Mi-28 helicopter; how a heavy machine gun is used in drone warfare; civilians fleeing the fighting were struck by artillery and mortar fire Trump’s America is becoming a rogue state. Ukraine, as well as Europe as a whole, must now accept that the United States is openly supporting Russia’s aggression against Ukraine. Under the pretext of efforts to end the war, the US government — and, as of Tuesday, a major technology company as well — are openly backing the fight against Ukraine and, therefore, against European security. The United States has recently taken several decisions in quick succession that could help Russia win the war, at a time when it was failing to do so on the battlefield. US president Donald Trump eased sanctions on trade in Russian oil, enabling Russian president Vladimir Putin to better finance his aggression against Ukraine, and effectively called for the overthrow of Ukraine’s legitimate president. A growing number of voices claim that the US has stopped providing intelligence on Russian air raids (this has not been confirmed, and some authorities deny it). And the United States has now also deprived the Ukrainian army of the ability to carry out effective medium-range strikes. It did so by dramatically restricting the Starlink service over Ukraine’s occupied territories. In practice, this will have serious consequences for the Ukrainian army’s ability to use drones for its previously highly effective attacks on Russian logistics. What the restrictions on Starlink mean and how they are being felt. Since this morning, the Ukrainian army has reported restrictions on the operation of receivers for SpaceX’s satellite system. Thanks to Starlink boss Elon Musk’s equipment, they destroy hundreds of Russian army trucks and other military equipment every month at distances of 30 to more than 100 km. However, on the night of 14 October , Ukrainians lost access to the military part of the system known as Starshield, meaning that the devices did not function at speeds above 160km/h. This means drones cannot carry out combat missions because their operators cannot guide them to their targets. The situation deteriorated further during the day. Serhii Sternenko reported that the army later reported losing control at speeds above 70 km/h. This means grounding Ukraine’s drone fleet for medium-range attacks. It is highly likely that this is not a technical problem but a response to a request from the Trump administration, since otherwise the Ukrainian army would have received an explanation — which, according to Ukrainian sources, did not happen. According to our observations, communications may have been interrupted for 10 to 20 seconds during drone flights,even at speeds of 110 to 120 kilometres per hour,” Oboronka news outlet quoted a military source. A technical problem is unlikely, as the Ukrainian military would have received an explanation in that case, which,according to Ukrainian sources, did not happen. The question now is how long the outage will last. It is also unclear to what extent the decision was made by Musk and to what extent by Trump. “Our defence forces received no warning of such a restriction, which led to the cancellation of several missions. It is clear that this is no coincidence and is connected to the current political situation,” wrote Serhii “Flash” Beskrestnov, for example. He described as an even more serious problem than the restriction of medium-range attacks the fact that Starlink is now crucial to intercepting Russian air raids on Ukrainian cities. “Through their actions, our partners are depriving us of one of the few means of protecting the country against jet-powered Shahed drones,” said Beskrestnov, a leading drone expert. Among European politicians, Poland’s foreign minister responded by asking Musk whether he was once again engaging in politics, and reminding him that his European customers were watching him closely. Naturally, the Russians are delighted. However, the change will not affect Ukrainian long-range air strikes. The drones carrying them out are not guided using Starlink, so the restrictions will not affect their operations. Hey, @elonmusk , big man, are you playing politics with your products again? As your European customers, we are watching you. https://t.co/T385xpUEUu — Radosław Sikorski 🇵🇱🇪🇺 (@sikorskiradek) October 14, 2026 The Russians are making a mockery of Trump’s energy ceasefire. The US president characteristically announced with great fanfare that he had brokered an energy ceasefire between Ukraine and Russia. Although the Russian army did not observe it for a single day, the Ukrainians stayed away from Russian refineries for 48 hours. That is no longer the case after today, but before then the Russians carried out a massive air raid, including on the capital. They used as many as 39 ballistic missiles and more than 100 drones. Since Trump had earlier deprived Ukraine of effective air defence in the form of missiles for Patriot systems, it has nothing with which to defend itself against such attacks. As a result, the Russians struck three Kyiv thermal power plants on Wednesday. Overnight, the Russians used 39 ballistic missiles and more than 120 attack drones and loitering munitions against our energy and critical infrastructure in Kyiv, the Kyiv region, and Kharkiv. It also included a list of the power plants hit. The Russians boasted that they had struck six of them. For each one, they used the formula that it was “supplying electricity to military logistics facilities, weapons depots and military equipment”. articles.title: House Democrats Push FAA to Pause AI Air Traffic Tools
articles.content: Lawmakers are continuing to question the Federal Aviation Administration’s rollout of its AI-powered aviation data tool, called the Strategic Management of Airspace Routes and Trajectories, or SMART. The tool debuted last month in a limited mode around the National Capital Region, spanning Baltimore/Washington International Thurgood Marshall Airport, Dulles International Airport and Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport. The goal is to provide aviation specialists with a centralized view of 200 data streams to help cut down on flight delays and cancellations.  In a letter sent Tuesday, most of the Democrats within the House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure asked the Government Accountability Office to investigate the FAA’s safety risk management activities tied to SMART and related platforms, identify the FAA’s quantifiable performance metrics used for evaluations and assess the development and deployment strategy. “The use of artificial intelligence within SMART has rightfully raised serious questions about its reliability and safety benefits, particularly on its potential to interfere with decision-making by experienced air traffic controllers or to hallucinate safety-critical information,” the members said . Last week, more than two dozen House Democrats sent a letter to Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford, urging the officials to pause use of the tool until questions around safety testing, implementation and oversight were answered.  “I support modernizing our aviation systems, but passenger safety must come first,” Maryland’s April McClain Delaney, who co-led the letter, said in a statement Friday. “I’m calling on the FAA to pause this rollout, show us the safety testing, and explain who is accountable when something goes wrong.” The group of congressional leaders characterized the tool’s rollout as “rush[ed]” and said it was launched “surprisingly” and “recklessly.” The letter also highlighted reported concerns about the tool from aviation workers and the airline industry .  “We have heard from several sources that frontline aviation safety workers were notified of the SMART tool rollout mere days in advance or not at all, giving them no time to learn how the system works, how it is incorporated into their workflow, and what oversight and accountability mechanisms maintain aviation safety standards,” per the letter.  Rep. Don Beyer of Virginia, one of the letter’s signatories and co-leads, was quick to express skepticism about the AI system, calling for the DOT unit to “ immediately suspend use ” on the day the tool launched. Some of his worries were alleviated after a conversation with Bedford, NextGov reported , though his support of the letter suggests at least some of the concerns lingered.   “Before deploying its AI-enabled SMART air traffic control tool, the FAA must demonstrate, through air traffic controller feedback and independently verified testing, that this technology is safe and reliable, and it must clearly communicate those findings to the public,” Beyer said in a statement accompanying last week’s letter.  Public concern surrounding AI is on the rise — and top of mind for congressional leaders and agency heads .  As part of the SMART platform launch, Duffy and Bedford repeated phrases about human workers continuing to be the ultimate decision-makers.  “There’s been a lot of conversation about AI and who’s controlling the airspace,” Duffy said during the launch event last month. “It’s always going to be a human that manages the airspace in America. This tool won’t manage airspace, but it gives us better information, better data to manage the airspace.”

articles.title: US Federal Contracts Drop Degree Requirements, Enable AI
articles.content: Congress recently sent to the president’s desk the Skills-Based Federal Contracting Act , a bill that stops agencies from writing minimum education requirements into contract solicitations unless they justify them in writing, directing them to assess skills instead.  The bill has been described as a jobs measure. It is also a change to what the government specifies when it buys services. As an economist who builds AI products, I think that change matters more than the jobs. When the federal government buys services, the contract usually describes the people who will do the work. Many labor categories name a degree and years of experience, and the contractor bills for those people by the hour. This gives the buyer some assurance about quality, and it sets a floor under the price, because no one can deliver the service for less than it costs to employ people who meet the specification. The act removes the degree from that list. A degree requirement is also, in effect, a requirement that a certain kind of person does the work. Without it, the government is closer to buying the work itself, and that work can now be done with far fewer people. A small team using AI tools, with someone accountable for the output, can often meet the same standard at a much lower cost. When that kind of delivery is allowed, the floor under the price drops, and it drops a long way. This small change could have large unintended consequences. First, the case for paying by the hour gets weaker. If a firm using AI can produce in two hours what used to take 10, a contract that pays for hours rewards the slower method. Part of what justified the rate for each labor category was the degree reinforcing it. Take the degree away and the rate is harder to defend. An agency that wants the lower price will need to buy a defined piece of work at a fixed price, and say clearly how it will judge whether the work is good enough. The act does not require agencies to do this, but it makes that easier. Second, the act changes the terms of competition. Many large incumbents are built around benches of junior staff billed by the hour, and degree requirements suited that model. With them gone, evaluations can give more weight to how the work will be done and what it will cost, which opens space for firms whose delivery relies on AI and small teams. Whether those firms win depends on the other barriers they face, including past performance and clearances, and on how quickly the large firms change their own delivery models. Third, the effects reach beyond the United States. Other governments have already moved further on credentials. The United Kingdom and Australia price much of their digital and professional services work against skills frameworks, with little reference to degrees. But they still buy people by the day or the hour, through panels and rate cards built around roles and seniority. It is that habit of paying for time that AI makes harder to defend, and the degree was only one part of it. The United States is one of the world’s largest buyers of services, so other governments pay attention to how it buys. If U.S. agencies show they can buy a defined piece of work for less, at a quality they are satisfied with, governments that have already dropped the degree will have to decide whether to keep paying for time. Firms that sell time to those governments will have to rethink how they price their work. The act was written to open federal work to people without degrees. Its larger effect may be to open it to firms that use AI to do the same work with far fewer people. Laurie Nicol is an economist, founder of Tendl, an AI company that assists companies in bidding, and author of The Venture Economist.

articles.title: Microsoft Disrupts Chinese Phishing Ecosystem
articles.content: Microsoft collaborated with Japanese authorities, Health-ISAC and several cybersecurity companies to dismantle an expansive, seemingly disconnected ecosystem of Chinese-language cybercrime tools and services, the company announced Wednesday. Since the start of the year, a vast collection of customized phishing kits developed and sold by Chinese-speaking threat actors — a cluster Microsoft tracks as Storm-2990 — have delivered more than 1 billion phishing emails and SMS messages to more than 75,000 organizations globally. More than three-quarters of those malicious messages targeted Microsoft customers, the company said. Cybercriminals purchased the phishing kits, tools and infrastructure from an interconnected network Microsoft and Japanese authorities started investigating in early 2025. The kits were used to target individuals and organizations in healthcare, financial services, logistics and IT predominantly in the United States and Japan. Microsoft said it and Health-ISAC, working with a federal court order, seized and redirected domains that powered the underlying infrastructure of these cybercrime tools and services known as YAM Store, CoGUI and Iron Man.  The company said it also disabled more than 20,000 accounts connected to YAM Store and continues to disrupt the operation by removing infrastructure hosted on its services and blocking more than 100,000 domains used for impersonation and fraud. “Most people have opened their messages to find a suspicious alert urgently telling them that a package cannot be delivered, a toll remains unpaid , a bank account needs attention, or a tax bill is overdue. The details may change, but the goal is the same: to get someone to click, share personal information, or pay,” Steven Masada, general counsel and general manager of Microsoft’s Digital Crimes Unit, wrote in a blog post. “These messages are relentless,” he added. “Delete and block one, and another takes its place. Ignore them, and more will follow. Fall for one, and the floodgates open. What appears to be a simple scam message is often the visible end of a much larger transnational cybercriminal operation.” The phishing kids included templates impersonating legitimate brands that cybercriminals used to facilitate high-volume campaigns. Researchers said similar infrastructure and overlapping activity suggested the tools shared development origins, code reuse or close collaboration among developers. Microsoft said cybercriminals used the phishing kits to steal credentials, financial data and abuse the device code authentication process to obtain authentication tokens and access compromised accounts. Researchers said cybercriminals primarily used the tools for financial fraud, typically using stolen payment data to make fraudulent purchases of high-end goods or transactions on legitimate financial platforms.  Resecurity, which aided the investigation, gained access to Iron Man’s infrastructure and found 2,360 phishing templates impersonating banks, retailers, healthcare providers, transportation authorities, police departments and government agencies across 130 countries. Cloudflare, Oracle, Proofpoint and TRM Labs also provided research and investigative support. “What began with scam activity targeting people and organizations in Japan led investigators to an underground service economy supplying criminals around the world,” Masada wrote.  “YAM Store, CoGUI and Iron Man are only part of that larger criminal network, but disrupting them makes it harder for criminals to obtain the accounts, tools and infrastructure they rely on,” he added. “The scam message is often the only part victims see. The businesses behind it are what make it possible.”

articles.title: Nvidia, Cisco Partner for Fatter, Faster Pluggables
articles.content: If you thought 1.6 Tbps was fast, just wait, Cisco's USFP targets 12.8 Tbps in a single optical pluggable Tobias Mann Tobias Mann SYSTEMS EDITOR Published wed 14 Oct 2026 // 14:30 UTC Make us preferred on Google Cisco make-me-root email bug exploited as a 0-day by unknown crims 4 hours ago Linux kernel devs drop obligatory confession of AI tool usage 6 hours ago Researchers cig-nal their faith in AI by taking up smoking 10 hours ago Tiny11 puts Windows 11 on a diet without the PowerShell workout 12 hours ago The AI math isn't mathing as infrastructure spending forecast to outstrip expected revenue 17 hours ago AI datacenters are a rats nest of fiber optic cables stitching together thousands of AI accelerators, NICs, switches, and everything else required to train and run the latest and greatest modes. Cisco hopes to untangle this mess with a new pluggable optic developed in collaboration with Nvidia that will pack between four and eight times the bandwidth of existing pluggables into a single port. Announced at the Open Compute Project (OCP) global summit this week, the ultra-dense small form factor pluggable ( USFP ) promises to pack up to 32, 400 Gbps lanes into a pluggable roughly the size of existing OSFP modules. Each of these pluggables would boast 12.8 Tbps of Ethernet bandwidth, as much as a high-end enterprise switch just a few years ago. To put that in perspective, the most sophisticated pluggable optics today cap out at around 1.6 Tbps using eight 200 Gbps links. Such a pluggable has the potential to significantly simplify cabling across AI datacenters where it isn't uncommon for each GPU to be paired with an 800 Gbps and soon 1.6 Tbps NIC. A single USFP pluggable could consolidate eight GPUs worth of cabling into a single fiber optic bundle. Meanwhile, on the switch side, a future 204.8 Tbps switch would only require 16 USFP ports to support 128 1.6 Tbps endpoints. Cramming all that connectivity into a single pluggable won't be easy. Today a high-end pluggable optic might pull on the order of 20 watts. Cisco's USFP spec calls for up to 100 watts per pluggable. There are also design constraints that have to be taken into consideration. Four times as many links per pluggable means 4x as many electrical contacts that have to be perfectly seated. Because of this Cisco says USFP modules will employ a two phase insertion mechanism in which the pluggable is first inserted into the cage and then a second mechanism is actuated to make the electrical connection. Speaking of reliability, USFP would have a bigger blast radius than conventional pluggables. A single bad laser or digital signal processor (DSP) has the potential to take out far more than a single GPU, but entire systems. While that might sound bad, it's nothing compared to co-packed or near-package optics where one failure could drop an entire rack's worth of accelerators from the network. Nvidia's participation in the development of the USFP standard is notable as the Ethernet networking titan has largely moved away from pluggables in its most recent set of switches. Many of its Spectrum-X and Quantum-X switches now use co-packaged optics and for good reason. Cutting out the pluggables on the switch side nets a roughly 30 percent power savings. But while Nvidia's latest switches may use CPO, its NICs still rely on pluggables in part because it offers integrators greater flexibility. Not everyone is building 100,000-plus GPU clusters for training. For racks utilizing a top of rack switch, lower power direct attach copper cabling can be used without much issue. Given Nvidia's investments in CPO we can only speculate on its interests in USFP, but it likely comes down to densification. The AI infrastructure giant is rapidly moving toward 600 kW racks packing 144 GPUs on board. First teased in early 2025, Nvidia's Vera Rubin Ultra platform promised 115.2 TB/s scale out bandwidth per rack or about 3.2-6.4 Tbps of bandwidth per GPU package depending on whether they're counting bidirectional bandwidth or not. It just so happens that Cisco's initial USFP spec calls for 16, 400 Gbps links per pluggable, or about 6.4 Tbps of bandwidth. While Cisco and Nvidia may be leading the charge on the development of an ultra dense optical pluggable, like most things Ethernet, USFP will be an open standard anyone can use in their designs. Microsoft taps Cisco for multi-datacenter AI Alongside Cisco's latest tie up with Nvidia, Switchzilla also revealed that Microsoft is now using its Silicon One P200 routing chips to distribute workloads across multiple datacenters. Nvidia and others have taken to calling this kind of multi-site computing: scale across networking . We discussed Cisco's datacenter-scale routing platform at length late last year, but the silicon competes directly with products like Nvidia's Spectrum-XGS and Broadcom's Jericho 4-based offerings. Cisco touts the P200 as the first 51.2 Tbps systems "deployed in a production environment by leading hyperscalers." With enough qualifiers you can be the first at anything. As we reported at the time, Microsoft was among the first major hyperscalers to embrace scale-across networking as a means of overcoming local power constraints with its Fairwater clusters in Wisconsin and Georgia. And it seems we finally know the hardware good old Redmond is using to stitch them together. Cisco gives SONiC some love Speaking of hyperscalers, one thing you probably won't find in a hyperscale network is Cisco's Nexus network operating system (NOS). Hyperscalers like Microsoft typically employ vendor agnostic NOS platforms to avoid vendor lock-in and make managing networks across multiple Ethernet vendors cheaper and easier. Originally developed by Microsoft and later open sourced, SONiC is among the most popular and widely deployed of the hyperscale NOSes. SONiC support, we should note is nothing new for Cisco which contrary to popular belief is more than willing to sell you any one piece of its networking stack, assuming you've got a big enough purse — the hyperscalers certainly do. As such Cisco is one of the biggest contributors to the SONiC project. Instead of forcing customers to use its software stack, Cisco's approach to SONiC and the hyperscale is to extend the NOSes capabilities to better take advantage of ASIC's unique capabilities and allow for integration with its services. At OCP this week, Cisco announced support for its Live Protect platform in SONiC to make it easier for customers to keep up with security patches in the wild. This capacity is expected to roll out next year. ® cisco ai nvidia fiber optics datacenter microsoft networks Make us preferred on Google

articles.title: Senators Press Trump Admin on AI Safety, Security
articles.content: Members of Congress are pressing the Trump administration to expand the federal government’s role in securing artificial intelligence, wanting new safety standards and regulations, independent testing of models and more “aggressive” use of AI for defensive cybersecurity purposes. In a letter , Sens. Maria Cantwell, D-Wash., and Mike Rounds, R-S.D., said that multiple incidents of frontier AI models escaping sandbox protections and breaching real companies, organizations and governments necessitate a stronger federal role in regulating the technology. Recent revelations that hundreds, and possibly “tens of thousands,” of such incidents may have occurred for months without OpenAI’s staff detecting them makes the need for federal intervention even more urgent, the senators argued. “These incidents come as AI systems are becoming dramatically more capable at discovering software vulnerabilities, writing and executing code, using digital tools, and operating autonomously,” the senators wrote. The letter, addressed to Jay Clayton, director of national intelligence and new White House “AI czar” and Michael Kratsios, director of the Office of Science and Technology Policy, urges the federal government “to bring its full capacities to bear on this challenge, building a coordinated national response around standards, testing, auditing, and defensive AI.” The Center for Advancing Innovation and Standards for Super Intelligence (CAISSI), housed within the Department of Commerce, has become the Trump administration’s main body for evaluating and testing AI models. In the letter, the senators are seeking to expand the center’s resources and mandate. Under the Trump administration, testing of frontier models has been voluntary and focused on evaluating model capabilities, not restricting them. The administration has since said it has reached a safety testing framework with OpenAI, Anthropic and other AI companies to govern safety testing, but has not made the agreement public. The senators call for CAISSI to spearhead the development of “technically grounded and measurable standards and risk management frameworks for advanced AI safety and security.” Those standards would address potential risks like cyberattacks, automated attacks on critical infrastructure and other threats. “The standards should also address the security of the environments in which advanced AI systems are developed, trained, tested, and used internally, including protections against agents escaping testing environments, gaining unauthorized access to external systems, or taking actions beyond their intended permissions,” the senators wrote. The letter argues the center and federal technology hubs like the National Institute of Standards and Technology should hire additional expertise in AI, cybersecurity, model evaluation and national security. It also calls for a much broader community of independent and third-party testers. Currently, that testing is done almost entirely by AI companies and hand-selected auditors, like Model Evaluation and Threat Research (METR), Redwood Research and others. Last month, Chris Painter, president of METR, told Congress that the firm’s investigation of the Hugging Face hacking incident was at the invitation of OpenAI, which tightly controls which organizations and testers get access to its unreleased models. While they are permitted to publicize some findings, such as those that relate to potentially catastrophic risks to humanity, researchers are otherwise restricted from discussing other parts of their investigation through nondisclosure agreements. Additionally, Painter suggested that frontier companies are relying too heavily on their own technology, rather than technical controls, to monitor and restrain their models in testing. “Because of the scale and speed at which AI agents are deployed, companies depend on AI monitoring and controls instead of human supervision, to prevent unwanted agent behavior,” Painter said. “That is, monitoring of AI is now in large part done by other AI systems.” The senators call for CAISSI, national laboratories and the Department of Energy to become federal testing sites. There, the government would evaluate AI models for advanced cyber capabilities, biological or chemical threats, threats to critical infrastructure, sandbox evasion techniques and other autonomous rule-breaking behavior. They also want testing opened to universities, independent research organizations and “qualified third-party evaluators,” including private sector companies. Other federal bodies, like the National Security Agency, the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency and National Science Foundation can help develop new standards and testbeds for AI tools used in defensive cybersecurity that can then be shared across government and with the public. “The recent incidents make clear that the security infrastructure surrounding advanced AI must advance as quickly as the technology itself,” the senators wrote. “The United States has an opportunity to lead both sides of this challenge: building the standards, testing, and auditing infrastructure needed for increasingly powerful AI, while harnessing those same capabilities to make American networks harder to attack.” You can read the full letter here .

articles.title: EU Risks Funding Israeli Tech with 'NAZA-type' Violence
articles.content: The European Union has continued its scientific cooperation with Israeli firms and institutions implicated in genocide and apartheid throughout Israel’s three-year old assault on Gaza. Such complicity must stop. Israel has been associated with the €95.5bn Horizon Europe research and innovation programme (2021-2027), and, according to the European Commission’s detailed Horizon dashboard , the EU’s net contribution to Israel amounts to €1.02bn. While much of the funding supports legitimate research, the programme also channels substantial resources to Israeli universities and companies, some closely connected to Israel’s military and security apparatus.  Pointing to just such EU-Israel collaboration, Francesca Albanese’s UN report “From economy of occupation to economy of genocide” published last year, estimated EU research funding to Israeli entities at over €2.12bn since 2014.  Horizon Europe funds collaborative projects and European Research Council grants. But it is the European Innovation Council (EIC) and schemes which include the EIC Accelerator, the EIC STEP Scale-up and the Scaleup Europe Fund which are especially relevant to the question of EU complicity in Israel’s ongoing assault on Gaza. Horizon Europe is formally limited to civilian research, but Israeli companies with links to Israel’s military and security establishment have received funding through these schemes.  In March 2026, for example, members of the European Parliament tabled a written parliamentary question asking the European Commission specifically about such companies including Sightec , an Israeli drone-navigation firm that received almost €2.5m through the EIC Accelerator and whose chief executive has described its technology as “combat-proven and deployed on over 3,000 drones in critical missions”. The issue is not confined to overtly military applications. EU-funded civilian technologies can also serve Israel’s settler-colonial project. Should European public money finance, for example, orange-harvesting robots that help Israel manage what it euphemistically calls a “labour shortage” in settlements built on occupied Palestinian land? The EIC also goes beyond grants. Through the EIC fund, the EU can take equity in companies it supports; the new Scaleup Europe Fund is explicitly designed to make direct equity investments in strategic technology firms, and is open to companies based in countries associated with Pillar III of Horizon Europe, including Israel. The EU can therefore not only subsidise Israeli technology firms but also acquire a financial stake in them and potentially profit from their future growth.  And it could get worse. The EIC’s 2026 work programme expands the type of projects that can be funded by including ‘dual use’ applications that are both civilian and military. This opens the door for the EU to fund nuclear-related Israeli projects although Israel is not a member of the European Atomic Energy community (Euratom). But none of this is inevitable. Israel’s association with the current Horizon Europe programme runs only until 2027 and the shape and scale of the EU’s next Horizon programme will be decided during ongoing negotiations on the bloc’s seven-year Multiannual Financial Framework (MFF). There are also clear signs that Israel is likely to participate in the next Horizon programme (2028-2034). Only a few weeks ago, Ekaterina Zaharieva, European commissioner for startups, research and innovation, met with the head of the Israel Space Agency, Shimrit Mama. Reportedly, they discussed potential cooperation in high-tech air defence and space capabilities, AI and robotics , and underlined the importance of satellite imaging, AI modelling and a “multi-layer defence approach.” European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen and her team must ask themselves if the EU should be building an innovation architecture in which Israeli firms and state institutions, which are already deeply integrated into Israel’s military-industrial ecosystem, could receive European support for technologies explicitly framed as dual-use or defence-related. Are they comfortable with funding companies that help develop the type of violent technologies described in the award-winning documentary NAZA , which exposes the systems and AI technology used during the military campaign in Gaza? Audience members hold signs supporting Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor’s documentary Naza after it wins the European Film Audience Award at the 74th San Sebastian Film Festival in Spain, 26 September 2026 (Source: EPA/JUAN HERRERO) Last year, under public pressure, von der Leyen proposed a partial suspension of Israel’s participation in Horizon Europe by specifically excluding Israeli entities from new EIC Accelerator grants and investment support.  The proposal was modest: it would have affected future funding only, not existing agreements, and covered roughly 20 percent of EU financial flows to Israel under the programme. It required a qualified majority in the Council but did not secure the necessary votes. It is, however, technically “still on the table”, according to commissioner Zaharieva . Nobel Peace Prize winner Navi Pillay concluded in 2025 that Israel’s actions have “consistently pointed toward a singular, harrowing objective – the destruction of Palestinian life in Gaza”. The EU has done little so far to stop the genocide in Gaza and ethnic cleansing in the occupied West Bank, and arguably - through trade and weapons’ exports - is actually contributing to it.  Now the EU faces a clear choice. It can continue to fund, co-invest in and deepen research ties with an Israeli innovation sector increasingly oriented towards dual-use and defence technologies.  Or it can stand with the winner of the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize, draw a line and decide that there will be no Israeli participation in the next Horizon programme, no EU equity in Israeli firms, and no public money for technologies that may be used to sustain genocide, occupation, surveillance and war. The credibility of the EU and the values it proclaims depends on the choice it makes.  Unlock article and share

articles.title: US Energy Regulators Block Data Center Power Cuts
articles.content: Federal energy regulators shoot down grid operator’s plan to cut power to data centers during shortfalls by Rachel Frazin - 10/13/26 5:58 PM ET Link copied - 10/13/26 5:58 PM ET Link copied NOW PLAYING The nation’s energy regulators have shot down a bid from a regional grid operator to cut power to some large data centers during a supply shortfall — leaving the issue largely in the hands of states. Regional grid operator PJM, which manages the electric grid for several East Coast and Midwest states, proposed an ability to cut power to new large consumers when it’s facing a shortage.  Its proposal would have applied to large data centers that don’t bring their own power sources. However, the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) rejected PM’s proposal, saying it may violate the Federal Power Act. The commissioners wrote that the law “leaves to the states alone ‘any other sale’ — most notably any retail sale” of electricity. The ruling comes after bipartisan governors and the Trump administration pushed PJM to do more to address rising electricity prices, in which data centers’ massive electricity demand is a factor.  Jeff Dennis, senior counsel at consulting firm Co2efficient, said that the decision puts pressure on states to set their own policy. Dennis, a former FERC staffer, said that the policies that states put in place could differ significantly. He said that “adds to the number of things that the states and that PJM and to some degree, still FERC, have to sort out” to avoid high power prices and blackouts in the future. PJM spokesperson Jeff Shields said in an email that the grid operator is “reviewing the Commission’s order with an eye toward how we can fulfill FERC’s requirements while recognizing the responsibilities FERC indicated belong to the states and honoring the concept that existing electricity customers should not be unfairly burdened by new, energy intensive customers in the form of higher costs or decreased reliability.” Add as preferred source on Google Tags AI data centers AI data centers Co2efficient data centers data centers Federal Energy Regulatory Commission FERC PJM Copyright 2026 Nexstar Media Inc. articles.title: Western Law Enforcement Disrupts West African Scam Network
articles.content: Global law enforcement agencies, tech firms disrupt West African scam network by Miranda Nazzaro - 10/13/26 6:04 PM ET Link copied - 10/13/26 6:04 PM ET Link copied NOW PLAYING A group of law enforcement agencies from around the world teamed up with a handful of high-profile technology firms to disrupt West African criminal scam networks, the Justice Department (DOJ) announced Tuesday. The operation led to “dozens” of arrests and 117 trafficking victims rescued from scam compounds in Ghana, the DOJ said . Authorities in the country seized hundreds of electronic devices, and at least $11 million was identified in potentially freezable funds Teams with the DOJ, FBI and other U.S. federal agencies convened at the National Crime Agency (NCA) in London to exchange intelligence about a transnational criminal scam network with cybercrime authorities around the world, including those in Ghana and Nigeria. Authorities teamed up with more than a dozen technology firms — such as Meta, OpenAI, Microsoft, Google, Starlink and Coinbase — to shut down linked accounts and stop active scams before they occurred. Meta said in a blog post it removed more than 3.7 million accounts, pages or groups accused of targeting users in the U.S. and United Kingdom. Most of these profiles impersonated American and British users. Microsoft suspended accounts suspected of being linked to the cybercrime, while Coinbase helped identify more than 65 victims and stopped more than $415,000 in potential scams, according to Meta. “These victims had been forced to work for scam operations by criminal syndicates and were rescued from imprisonment in a residential compound,” Meta wrote Tuesday. “The victims were malnourished and subjected to both physical and psychological abuses by their captors, who were arrested and are facing prosecution.” The scam network used various tactics to lure victims into giving money, according to Meta and prosecutors. This included persuading victims into fraudulent investment schemes, offering fake employee opportunities or digital tasks, or posing as law enforcement, military or government officials. It also involved criminals building fake romantic or professional relationships to lure victims into sending money. Law enforcement agencies from Australia, Canada, India and New Zealand, as well as Interpol, assisted in the investigation. “Fraud is a global problem and it takes partnership working across international boundaries to tackle it,” Nick Sharp, NCA deputy director of fraud, said in the DOJ’s press release. “Hosting such a rich and dedicated team of law enforcement and technology companies at NCA’s headquarters enabled us to utilize the power of partnerships and strike back at a significant set of criminals who inflict misery on thousands of victims of fraud.” Add as preferred source on Google Tags Copyright 2026 Nexstar Media Inc. articles.title: Epic Games Launcher Claims Superior Speed Over Steam
articles.content: Text settings Story text Size Small Standard Large Width * Standard Wide Links Standard Orange * Subscribers only    Learn more Minimize to nav Nearly eight years after Epic took on Steam with its own Game Store and launcher, the Fortnite maker is deploying a new tool to give it an edge over Valve: vibe coding. In announcing the new publicly available “Preview” build of its Epic Games Launcher, Epic writes that “programming is hard. So, instead of doing that, we vibe coded a new Epic Games Launcher that’s way faster and more responsive than the current one, and has a new look.” And while that might sound a little tongue-in-cheek, Epic Games Store General Manager and VP Martin Keely told PC Gamer that the team “started from scratch” and used AI as “a tool to write and review new features and new capabilities from the ground up in a different tech stack than what we had previously.” The goal, Keely said, was to “look at functionality that existed [in the current Epic Games Launcher] and [say] we want to replicate that, but not the code itself.” Speaking to IGN , Keely clarified that using AI to code the new Launcher “made us more efficient and allowed a small team to rewrite the code base and be able to launch it faster across platforms, support Windows and Mac, and we’re going to have a Linux version as well.” We vibe coded the Epic Games Launcher to be faster than the other guy. Don’t believe us? Test it out for yourself in Preview: https://t.co/pdtAeEIri4 https://t.co/aMxojUUVPV — Epic Games Store (@EpicGames) October 14, 2026 The focus on startup speed extends to Epic’s social media announcement , which once again stresses that “we vibe coded the Epic Games Launcher to be faster than the other guy.” Ars’s own testing confirms that the new Launcher goes from a cold start to the store page a few seconds faster than Steam (assuming no login or update issues get in the way). Epic also claims the new Launcher can restore from the system tray to the Library screen slightly faster than Steam, though the claimed difference of 0.06 seconds in this seems so small as to be unnoticeable (and was in our testing). Harder, better, faster, stronger Epic announced a ground-up “storefront rearchitecture” and “Launcher V2 private Beta” in an Unreal Fest presentation in June . At the time, the company said the new Launcher would have “5x faster cold start” times and help solve challenges that “every developer in this room and every player” has experienced with the current Launcher. The term “vibe coding” still carries heavy connotations of quickly thrown-together slop that could hide crucial errors beneath the surface. On social media, Epic warns that its Launcher Preview “will have some bugs” that early testers can help squash with a feedback form. The announcement post also warns that the vibe-coded Preview is currently “light on features”— an FAQ clarifies that “certain social features and account management options” haven’t made it over from the legacy version just yet. That said, the new Preview launcher adds some long-requested features like a Recent Games list and a centralized downloads hub for tracking network activity. And Epic writes that it is “working toward feature parity” between the new Launcher and the old one. Epic’s release of the new “vibe coded” Launcher preview comes just days after a Bloomberg report suggesting the company is pivoting to an “AI first” development model for an upcoming Star Wars and Marvel-themed shooter. “We have a huge pivot underway here at Epic, moving developers around to retool for maximum AI acceleration,” Epic CEO Tim Sweeney wrote on social media on Monday. “The aim isn’t to do the same stuff with fewer people, but to enable everyone here to build MORE and BETTER stuff, and to bring the benefits to all teams using Unreal.” Kyle Orland Senior Gaming Editor Kyle Orland Senior Gaming Editor . 105 Comments

articles.title: Hong Kong Smog Persists, 'Serious' Health Risk Warned
articles.content: Unhealthy levels of air pollution have persisted across parts of Hong Kong on Wednesday, after the Environmental Protection Department (EPD) recorded a “serious” level of health risk at monitoring stations on Tuesday. Air pollution across Hong Kong on Wednesday, October 14, 2026. Photo: aqicn.org. However, the Observatory said a fresh easterly airstream will arrive at the coast of Guangdong on Wednesday, helping to dissipate the smog. “Winds are weak over Hong Kong this afternoon, which are unfavourable for pollutant dispersion,” the EPD said in a Tuesday press release. “The intense sunshine enhances photochemical smog activity, leading to the rapid formation of ozone and fine particulates in the Pearl River Delta region. The high ozone level also promotes the formation of nitrogen dioxide.” See also: Bookmark weatherhongkong.com for weather and air quality updates According to aqicn.org, which draws upon official data, the Air Quality Index reached 154 in Causeway Bay on Wednesday morning, classified as “unhealthy.” Much of the rest of the territory saw high levels of pollution, classified as “unhealthy for sensitive groups.” The EPD’s health risk categories range between “low” and “serious” – the highest level – and track the presence of pollutants including PM2.5 particulates in the atmosphere. “At the ‘Serious’ level, employers of all outdoor workers are advised to assess the risk of outdoor work and take appropriate preventive measures to protect the health of their employees,” the department said. Webcams across Hong Kong as of Wednesday, October 14, 2026. Photo: HKO. PM2.5 refers to atmospheric particulate matter measuring less than 2.5 micrometres- about 3 per cent of the diameter of a human hair. As one of the most common units of air quality measurement, studies link PM2.5 to premature mortality, heart or lung diseases, asthma attacks, acute and chronic bronchitis, and other respiratory illnesses. The main sources of local pollution are marine vessels, motor vehicles and power plants. University of Hong Kong researchers estimate that, in 2024, air pollution led to 3,508 premature deaths in the city and economic losses of HK$42 billion. Those who live in socially deprived areas are more exposed to higher-than-average air pollution levels, an earlier study found. Worldwide, air pollution is linked to 6.7 million premature deaths every year, according to the World Health Organization.
